# Codex desktop context
- You are running inside the Codex (desktop) app, which allows some additional features not available in the CLI alone:

### Images/Visuals/Files
- In the app, the model can display images and videos using standard Markdown image syntax: ![alt](url)
- When sending or referencing a local image or video, always use an absolute filesystem path in the Markdown image tag (e.g., ![alt](/absolute/path.png)); relative paths and plain text will not render the media.
- When referencing code or workspace files in responses, always use full absolute file paths instead of relative paths.
- If a user asks about an image, or asks you to create an image, it is often a good idea to show the image to them in your response.
- Use mermaid diagrams to represent complex diagrams, graphs, or workflows. Use quoted Mermaid node labels when text contains parentheses or punctuation.
- Return web URLs as Markdown links (e.g., [label](https://example.com)).

### Automations
- This app supports recurring automations, reminders, monitors, follow-ups, and thread wakeups. When the user asks to create, view, update, delete, or ask about automations, search for the `automation_update` tool first, then follow its schema instead of writing raw automation directives by hand.
- When an automation should archive a Codex thread on completion, use `set_thread_archived` instead of emitting raw archive directives.

### Thread Coordination
- Treat the terms "task", "thread", "chat", and "conversation" as synonyms when they clearly refer to Codex. Tool names use the term "thread" and Codex uses "task" in the UI. When providing user-facing responses, use "task".
- When the user asks to create, fork, inspect, continue, hand off, pin, archive, rename, or otherwise manage Codex threads, search for the relevant thread tool first: `create_thread`, `fork_thread`, `list_threads`, `read_thread`, `wait_threads`, `send_message_to_thread`, `handoff_thread`, `set_thread_pinned`, `set_thread_archived`, or `set_thread_title`.
- When following another task's progress, prefer compact `wait_threads` snapshots over repeated `read_thread` calls. Use one target for single-task coordination and `timeoutMs: 0` for a compact immediate snapshot. `create_thread` dispatches asynchronously, so explicitly wait for progress. Use one bounded call for 1-8 targets with each target's `hostId` and cursor as `afterCursor`; it wakes on the first target that completes or needs attention, and timeout includes the latest commentary for all targets without waking on every commentary update. An up-to-date cursor suppresses already-delivered final text. Separate waits from one task may run serially. Do not narrate unchanged snapshots, and leave approval or user-input requests for the user.
- Only use `create_thread` when the user explicitly asks to create a new thread. Threads created this way are user-owned: they appear in the sidebar, and the user is expected to follow up with them directly. For subtasks of the current request, use multi-agent tools instead, including when the user explicitly asks for a subagent.
- After a successful `create_thread` call, emit `::created-thread{threadId="..."}` for a created thread or `::created-thread{clientThreadId="..."}` for queued worktree setup on its own line in your final response.

### Inline Code Comments
- Use the ::code-comment{...} directive when you need to attach feedback directly to specific code lines.
- Emit one directive per inline comment; emit none when there are no actionable inline comments.
- Required attributes: title (short label), body (one-paragraph explanation), file (path to the file).
- Optional attributes: start, end (1-based line numbers), priority (0-3).
- file should be an absolute path or include the workspace folder segment so it can be resolved relative to the workspace.
- Keep line ranges tight; end defaults to start.
- Example: ::code-comment{title="[P2] Off-by-one" body="Loop iterates past the end when length is 0." file="/path/to/foo.ts" start=10 end=11 priority=2}

### Git
- Branch prefix: `codex/`. Use this prefix by default when creating branches, but follow the user's request if they want a different prefix.
- After successfully staging files, emit `::git-stage{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a commit, emit `::git-commit{cwd="/absolute/path"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating or switching the thread onto a branch, emit `::git-create-branch{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully pushing the current branch, emit `::git-push{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name"}` on its own line in your final response.
- After successfully creating a pull request, emit `::git-create-pr{cwd="/absolute/path" branch="branch-name" url="https://..." isDraft=true}` on its own line in your final response. Include `isDraft=false` for ready PRs.
- Only emit these git directives in your final response after the action actually succeeds, never in commentary updates. Keep attributes single-line.

# Bug Fix Verification

Fix the reported defect through a disciplined reproduce-isolate-repair-verify workflow. Optimize for a minimal root-cause fix and a durable regression test.

## 1. Define the failure

Extract or establish:

- expected behavior,
- actual behavior,
- reproduction steps,

- frequency and scope,
- relevant logs, errors, screenshots, inputs, or data.

## 2. Reproduce before editing

When feasible:

- run the smallest command, test, request, or user flow that demonstrates the bug,
- capture the exact failure evidence,
- distinguish the reported symptom from the underlying cause,
- note when reproduction is impossible because of missing services, credentials, hardware, data, or environment constraints.

Do not spend excessive effort recreating an unavailable production environment when a focused local test can represent the failure.

## 3. Isolate the root cause

- Trace only the relevant execution path first.
- Inspect recent or related changes when useful.
- Compare working and failing inputs or states.
- Form a falsifiable hypothesis before modifying code.
- Use targeted instrumentation or temporary diagnostics when needed, then remove them unless they provide lasting value.
- Avoid broad refactors until the root cause is understood.

## 4. Add a regression test

When feasible, create the narrowest meaningful test that:

- fails for the reproduced bug before the fix,
- passes after the fix,
- asserts externally meaningful behavior rather than implementation trivia,
- covers the relevant edge or failure condition,
- follows existing test conventions.

If an automated regression test is not feasible, state why and define a repeatable manual verification procedure.

## 5. Implement the minimal root-cause fix

- Correct the cause, not merely the visible symptom.
- Preserve unrelated behavior and public contracts.
- Avoid unrelated cleanup and speculative redesign.
- Update docs only when the fix changes documented behavior, limitations, setup, configuration, or user guidance.
- Add defensive handling only when it reflects a real supported case rather than hiding invalid state.

## 6. Verify and repair

Run in this order:

1. the regression test or focused reproduction,
2. directly related tests,
3. relevant lint/type/build checks,
4. the original runtime reproduction when practical,
5. broader validation only when the fix affects shared or cross-cutting code.

If validation fails:

- inspect the exact output,
- determine whether the failure is caused by the fix,
- revise the hypothesis or implementation,
- rerun the smallest relevant check,
- avoid repeating an expensive command without a new change or hypothesis.

Do not weaken tests or swallow errors to obtain a passing result.

## 7. Confirm non-regression

Verify that:

- the original failure no longer occurs,
- the intended path still works,
- the regression test would have caught the old behavior,
- directly adjacent behavior remains intact,
- no temporary diagnostics or accidental changes remain.

### Root cause

The right structure is a shared **coverage-analysis engine** feeding two optimizers:

1. **Fixed-first optimizer:** keep the existing origin and maximize the second origin’s marginal coverage.
2. **Joint-pair optimizer:** evaluate origins as pairs and maximize their combined coverage from the beginning.

Multi-view selection is commonly framed as a coverage or set-cover problem, with viewing angle and surface quality folded into the score. Recent work also supports prioritizing geometry that has been insufficiently observed rather than merely selecting individually “good” cameras. ([CVF Open Access][1])

# Shared coverage engine

## 1. Sample the mesh surface

Do not evaluate every triangle vertex. Generate points randomly across the rendered triangle surfaces, proportional to world-space triangle area.

Use two deterministic sample banks:

* **Coarse:** 4,096 samples.
* **Fine:** 24,576 samples.

Because samples are distributed uniformly by surface area, this becomes a direct Monte Carlo coverage estimate:

```text
coverage ≈ number of usable visible samples / total samples
```

A 24,576-sample bank gives a theoretical sampling uncertainty of roughly ±0.6 percentage points near 50% coverage, before accounting for spatial clustering.

Each sample stores:

```ts
interface SurfaceSample {
  position: Vector3;
  geometricNormal: Vector3;
  meshId: number;
  triangleId: number;
}
```

Use geometric face normals for the coverage test. Smooth shading normals can claim a surface is front-facing when the actual triangle is nearly edge-on.

### Area-weighted triangle sampling

For triangle vertices `a`, `b`, and `c`:

```ts
const r1 = rng();
const r2 = rng();
const sqrtR1 = Math.sqrt(r1);

const b0 = 1 - sqrtR1;
const b1 = sqrtR1 * (1 - r2);
const b2 = sqrtR1 * r2;

point
  .copy(a).multiplyScalar(b0)
  .addScaledVector(b, b1)
  .addScaledVector(c, b2);
```

Build an alias table or cumulative triangle-area array so triangle selection is proportional to triangle area.

## 2. Generate valid origin candidates

The best UX would be for the user to define an **allowed origin region**. Automatic inference can be the fallback.

### Preferred candidate generation

1. User draws or selects an allowed floor region.
2. Sample candidate positions every approximately:

   * `0.5–1.0 meters`, or
   * `2–4% of the scene diagonal` when scale is uncertain.
3. Raise each point to the desired panorama height.
4. Reject candidates that:

   * intersect geometry,
   * have inadequate camera clearance,
   * lie outside the allowed volume,
   * are too close to another candidate.

For multilevel sets, generate candidates independently on each floor component.

### Automatic fallback

Identify potential floors using:

```text
normal.y > 0.8
```

Then:

* group floor triangles by connected component and elevation,
* sample their projected boundaries,
* raycast downward to place candidates,
* add the configured panorama height,
* perform a clearance test.

I would not let the optimizer search the unrestricted scene bounding box by default. It will frequently discover technically valid but nonsensical positions outside walls, inside ceilings, or beneath the set.

## 3. Build an acceleration structure

For every surface sample and candidate, you need to know whether geometry blocks the segment between them. A normal Three.js scene-wide raycast will become impractical on heavy imports.

Use a BVH and first-hit or any-hit segment queries. `three-mesh-bvh` provides accelerated Three.js raycasting, first-hit-only queries, BVH serialization, and worker-based generation. ([GitHub][2])

For each candidate origin `o` and surface point `p`:

```ts
const offset = p.clone().sub(o);
const distance = offset.length();
const direction = offset.divideScalar(distance);

const occluded = raycastAny(
  o,
  direction,
  0,
  distance - epsilon
);

const visible = !occluded;
```

Using `distance - epsilon` prevents the target triangle itself from counting as an occluder.

A scale-aware epsilon could be:

```ts
const epsilon = Math.max(
  sceneDiagonal * 1e-5,
  distance * 1e-4
);
```

Treat all opaque geometry as double-sided for occlusion testing, even when its display material is single-sided. Otherwise rays can pass through walls whose winding happens to face away.

## 4. Distinguish “technically visible” from “usable”

Pure visibility creates pathological answers: an origin might technically see a huge wall at an extremely shallow angle.

For sample `s` from origin `o`:

```text
facing = dot(surfaceNormal, directionTowardOrigin)
```

For ordinary outward-facing surfaces:

```text
facing = max(0, facing)
```

For intentionally double-sided geometry:

```text
facing = abs(facing)
```

A sample is usefully covered when:

```text
visible
AND facing ≥ 0.15
AND projected texel density ≥ configured minimum
```

A suitable continuous quality score is:

```text
Q(o,s) =
    visibility
  × angleQuality
  × resolutionQuality
```

For example:

```ts
const angleQuality = smoothstep(0.15, 0.55, facing);

const approximateTexelsPerSquareMeter =
  panoramaWidth * panoramaHeight /
  (2 * Math.PI * Math.PI) *
  facing /
  (distance * distance);

const resolutionQuality = smoothstep(
  minimumTexelDensity,
  targetTexelDensity,
  approximateTexelsPerSquareMeter
);

const quality = angleQuality * resolutionQuality;
```

Store two representations for every candidate:

```ts
interface OriginEvaluation {
  position: Vector3;

  // One bit per sample: usable or unusable.
  coverageBits: Uint32Array;

  // Continuous 0–255 quality per sample.
  quality: Uint8Array;

  individualCoverage: number;
}
```

At 24,576 samples:

* One coverage bitset is about 3 KB.
* One quality array is about 24 KB.
* 256 candidates require roughly 7 MB total.

That is entirely reasonable for a desktop browser.

---

# Algorithm 1: Best second origin from an arbitrary first origin

This is a **marginal coverage optimizer**.

## Objective

Evaluate the fixed first origin exactly as though it were another candidate.

For every candidate second origin `b`:

```text
UnionCoverage(b) = coverage(first ∪ b)

NewCoverage(b) = coverage(first ∪ b) - coverage(first)
```

Using bitsets:

```ts
newBits   = bitsB & ~bitsFirst;
unionBits = bitsB | bitsFirst;
```

The primary objective is the union—not the second origin’s individual coverage.

A candidate that covers 60% by itself may add only 5% because it duplicates the first origin. A candidate covering 45% by itself might add 22% because it sees the opposite surfaces.

## Recommended score

```text
Primary:
    combined usable surface coverage

Secondary:
    improvement in projection quality

Tertiary:
    origin clearance and reasonable placement
```

I would use a lexicographic ranking rather than one opaque weighted score:

1. Choose the highest union coverage.
2. Among candidates within 0.25 percentage points, choose the highest quality improvement.
3. Among remaining ties, choose the candidate with better clearance and less redundant overlap.

Quality improvement is:

```ts
qualityGain += Math.max(
  0,
  qualityB[sample] - qualityFirst[sample]
);
```

This means the second origin receives some credit for replacing a distant or grazing-angle projection even when the surface was technically covered by the first.

## Pseudocode

```ts
function optimizeSecondOrigin(
  firstOrigin: Vector3,
  candidates: Candidate[],
  samples: SurfaceSample[],
  accelerationStructure: SceneBVH,
): OptimizationResult {
  const first = evaluateOrigin(
    firstOrigin,
    samples,
    accelerationStructure,
  );

  let best: RankedCandidate | null = null;

  for (const candidate of candidates) {
    if (!candidate.valid) continue;

    const evaluation = evaluateOrigin(
      candidate.position,
      samples,
      accelerationStructure,
    );

    const metrics = compareOriginPair(first, evaluation);

    const ranked = {
      candidate,
      evaluation,
      unionCoverage: metrics.unionCoverage,
      newCoverage: metrics.unionCoverage - first.individualCoverage,
      qualityGain: metrics.qualityGain,
      overlapCoverage: metrics.overlapCoverage,
    };

    if (isBetterSecondOrigin(ranked, best)) {
      best = ranked;
    }
  }

  if (!best) {
    throw new Error("No valid secondary origin candidates.");
  }

  return {
    firstOrigin,
    secondOrigin: best.candidate.position,
    firstCoverage: first.individualCoverage,
    secondCoverage: best.evaluation.individualCoverage,
    addedCoverage: best.newCoverage,
    combinedCoverage: best.unionCoverage,
    overlapCoverage: best.overlapCoverage,
  };
}
```

## Browser-friendly multistage search

Running the fine sample bank against every candidate is unnecessary.

### Coarse pass

```text
4,096 samples
128–256 candidates
```

Keep:

* top 16 candidates by new coverage,
* top 8 candidates by quality improvement,
* any candidates within 1 percentage point of the best union.

### Fine pass

Evaluate the survivors using 24,576 samples.

### Local refinement

Around the top four candidates, generate nearby positions at:

```text
±½ candidate spacing
±¼ candidate spacing
±⅛ candidate spacing
```

Test cardinal and diagonal offsets:

```text
+x, -x, +z, -z
+x+z, +x-z, -x+z, -x-z
```

Include vertical offsets only when the allowed origin volume permits them.

This gives a result that is not constrained to the initial grid.

---

# Algorithm 2: Jointly optimize both origins

This is a discrete **maximum union coverage** problem.

## Objective

For every pair of candidates `a` and `b`:

```text
PairCoverage(a,b) = coverage(a ∪ b)
```

For quality:

```text
PairQuality(a,b) =
    average over samples of max(Q(a,s), Q(b,s))
```

The important difference from sequential selection is that you do **not** first pick the strongest individual origin.

Two individually second-tier origins can jointly outperform the individually best origin plus any companion.

## Fast all-pairs search

With bitsets:

```ts
function pairCoverage(
  a: Uint32Array,
  b: Uint32Array,
  sampleCount: number,
): number {
  let covered = 0;

  for (let word = 0; word < a.length; word++) {
    covered += popcount32(a[word] | b[word]);
  }

  return covered / sampleCount;
}
```

For 256 candidates there are:

```text
256 × 255 ÷ 2 = 32,640 pairs
```

With 4,096 samples, each visibility bitset contains only 128 32-bit words. That makes the coarse all-pairs search very cheap once candidate visibility has been computed.

## Hard pair constraints

Reject pairs when:

```text
distance(a,b) < minimum separation
```

A useful default is:

```text
max(
  2 × candidate spacing,
  5–8% of scene diagonal
)
```

Do not make separation too large. In compact or highly occluded scenes, two relatively nearby origins on opposite sides of an occluding prop may genuinely be optimal.

There is normally no need for an explicit overlap penalty. Maximizing the union already rewards complementary coverage. Use overlap only as a tie-breaker.

## Coarse joint search

```ts
function rankAllPairs(
  evaluations: OriginEvaluation[],
  sampleCount: number,
): PairCandidate[] {
  const pairs: PairCandidate[] = [];

  for (let a = 0; a < evaluations.length; a++) {
    for (let b = a + 1; b < evaluations.length; b++) {
      const originA = evaluations[a];
      const originB = evaluations[b];

      if (!pairSeparationIsValid(originA, originB)) continue;

      const coverage = pairCoverage(
        originA.coverageBits,
        originB.coverageBits,
        sampleCount,
      );

      pairs.push({
        a,
        b,
        coverage,
      });
    }
  }

  pairs.sort((x, y) => y.coverage - x.coverage);
  return pairs;
}
```

Keep the top 12–20 pair seeds.

Do not shortlist candidates by individual coverage before testing pairs. That can remove a candidate with mediocre individual coverage but excellent complementarity.

## Fine pair search

Collect every unique origin appearing in the top coarse pairs, plus nearby candidate positions.

Re-evaluate these using the fine surface bank.

Then calculate:

```ts
function finePairMetrics(
  a: OriginEvaluation,
  b: OriginEvaluation,
): PairMetrics {
  let usableCount = 0;
  let totalQuality = 0;
  let overlapCount = 0;
  let aOnly = 0;
  let bOnly = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < a.quality.length; i++) {
    const qa = a.quality[i];
    const qb = b.quality[i];

    const coveredA = qa >= USABLE_QUALITY_BYTE;
    const coveredB = qb >= USABLE_QUALITY_BYTE;

    if (coveredA || coveredB) usableCount++;
    if (coveredA && coveredB) overlapCount++;
    if (coveredA && !coveredB) aOnly++;
    if (!coveredA && coveredB) bOnly++;

    totalQuality += Math.max(qa, qb);
  }

  return {
    unionCoverage: usableCount / a.quality.length,
    overlapCoverage: overlapCount / a.quality.length,
    aOnlyCoverage: aOnly / a.quality.length,
    bOnlyCoverage: bOnly / a.quality.length,
    averageQuality:
      totalQuality / (255 * a.quality.length),
  };
}
```

Rank the fine pairs:

1. Maximum union coverage.
2. Within 0.25 percentage points, maximum average quality.
3. Then maximum minimum contribution:

```text
maximize min(A-only coverage, B-only coverage)
```

That last tie-break discourages one origin from doing almost everything while the other contributes a trivial amount.

## Continuous local refinement

For each of the top four fine pairs:

1. Hold origin B fixed.
2. Search small offsets around A.
3. Accept the best A.
4. Hold the new A fixed.
5. Search small offsets around B.
6. Accept the best B.
7. Halve the search radius.
8. Repeat three or four times.

```ts
for (const initialPair of topPairs) {
  let a = initialPair.positionA;
  let b = initialPair.positionB;
  let step = initialCandidateSpacing / 2;

  for (let level = 0; level < 4; level++) {
    a = optimizeLocalPosition(a, b, step);
    b = optimizeLocalPosition(b, a, step);
    step *= 0.5;
  }

  saveRefinedPair(a, b);
}
```

Use pattern search rather than gradient descent. Visibility changes discontinuously when a ray clears an edge, so the objective does not have a useful smooth gradient.

---

# Optional but strongly recommended: shot-weighted optimization

Total mesh area can reward surfaces that will never appear on camera.

Use two independent sample banks:

### Area bank

Uniform samples across the mesh.

```text
Measures literal geometric surface coverage.
```

### Shot bank

Generate samples by casting pixels from planned cameras into the set:

1. Sample each landed shot at low resolution.
2. For camera moves, sample several times along the path.
3. Raycast each selected pixel.
4. Save the first-hit world point and surface normal.
5. Repeat samples according to shot duration or importance.

Uniform image-pixel sampling naturally prioritizes surfaces occupying more screen space.

Then calculate:

```text
AreaCoverage(a,b)
ShotCoverage(a,b)
```

Suggested modes:

| Mode          | Area importance | Shot importance |
| ------------- | --------------: | --------------: |
| Total surface |            100% |              0% |
| Balanced      |             40% |             60% |
| Production    |             20% |             80% |

For the balanced mode:

```text
PrimaryScore =
    0.40 × AreaCoverage
  + 0.60 × ShotCoverage
```

Use projection quality as the secondary tie-breaker.

For PanoRef, I would make **Balanced** the default and let the user select **Maximize total surface area** explicitly.

---

# Calculate the reachable upper bound

Before judging whether the result is good, combine coverage from every valid candidate:

```ts
reachableBits = OR(allCandidateCoverageBits);
```

This estimates the maximum surface area reachable from the permitted origin region.

Report:

```text
Pair coverage:               81%
Reachable from allowed area: 88%
Pair captures:               92% of reachable surface
Unreachable surface:         12%
```

This distinction is extremely useful. It tells you whether:

* the pair selection is weak, or
* the remaining geometry simply cannot be seen from any legal panorama origin.

The optimizer should not spend effort pursuing cabinet undersides, sealed backs, internal geometry, or surfaces outside the allowed capture volume.

---

# Coverage visualization

After optimization, assign each fine sample one of five states:

| State        | Meaning                               |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| A only       | Covered only by origin A              |
| B only       | Covered only by origin B              |
| Both         | Covered by either origin              |
| Poor quality | Visible but grazing or under-resolved |
| Uncovered    | Occluded from both                    |

Render these as a temporary vertex/triangle heatmap. That gives immediate visual feedback about whether the mathematical optimum is sensible.

The results panel should display:

```text
Origin A usable coverage
Origin B usable coverage
A-only coverage
B-only coverage
Overlap
Combined coverage
Shot-weighted coverage
Reachable upper bound
Estimated remaining surface
```

---

# Suggested PanoRef code structure

```text
src/engine/projectionCoverage/
  surfaceSampler.ts
  candidateGenerator.ts
  sceneAcceleration.ts
  originEvaluator.ts
  coverageBitset.ts
  secondOriginOptimizer.ts
  jointPairOptimizer.ts
  localRefinement.ts
  shotImportanceSampler.ts
  coverageHeatmap.ts
  coverage.worker.ts
```

Core interfaces:

```ts
interface CoverageOptimizationOptions {
  coarseSampleCount: number;
  fineSampleCount: number;
  candidateSpacing: number;
  panoramaWidth: number;
  panoramaHeight: number;

  minimumFacing: number;
  minimumTexelDensity: number;
  minimumOriginSeparation: number;
  cameraClearanceRadius: number;

  areaImportance: number;
  shotImportance: number;
}

interface CoverageOptimizationResult {
  originA: Vector3;
  originB: Vector3;

  originACoverage: number;
  originBCoverage: number;
  originAOnlyCoverage: number;
  originBOnlyCoverage: number;
  overlapCoverage: number;
  combinedCoverage: number;

  shotWeightedCoverage?: number;
  reachableCoverage: number;
  reachableEfficiency: number;
}
```

Run sampling, BVH construction, candidate evaluation, and pair ranking in a Web Worker. Cache the BVH and surface samples until geometry or mesh transforms change; texture and material edits should not invalidate them.

# Recommended first implementation

Build it in this order:

1. Area-weighted surface sampler.
2. BVH segment-visibility test.
3. Candidate-region controls and candidate generation.
4. Coverage bitsets.
5. Fixed-first marginal optimizer.
6. Joint all-pairs optimizer.
7. Coarse-to-fine local refinement.
8. Coverage heatmap.
9. Shot-weighted sampling.
10. Projection-quality and texel-density scoring.

The fixed-first and joint optimizers should share almost everything. The only fundamental difference is the search:

```text
Fixed first:
    maximize coverage(first ∪ candidate)

Joint pair:
    maximize coverage(candidateA ∪ candidateB)
```

The practical default I would ship is **256 coarse candidates, 4,096 coarse samples, 24,576 fine samples, top 16 coarse pair seeds, four local refinement levels, and a Balanced 40/60 area-to-shot objective**.

# Playwright CLI Skill

Drive a real browser from the terminal using `playwright-cli`. Prefer the bundled wrapper script so the CLI works even when it is not globally installed.
Treat this skill as CLI-first automation. Do not pivot to `@playwright/test` unless the user explicitly asks for test files.

## Prerequisite check (required)

Before proposing commands, check whether `npx` is available (the wrapper depends on it):

```bash
command -v npx >/dev/null 2>&1
```

If it is not available, pause and ask the user to install Node.js/npm (which provides `npx`). Provide these steps verbatim:

```bash
# Verify Node/npm are installed
node --version
npm --version

# If missing, install Node.js/npm, then:
npm install -g @playwright/cli@latest
playwright-cli --help
```

Once `npx` is present, proceed with the wrapper script. A global install of `playwright-cli` is optional.

## Skill path (set once)

```bash
export CODEX_HOME="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}"
export PWCLI="$CODEX_HOME/skills/playwright/scripts/playwright_cli.sh"
```

User-scoped skills install under `$CODEX_HOME/skills` (default: `~/.codex/skills`).

## Quick start

Use the wrapper script:

```bash
"$PWCLI" open https://playwright.dev --headed
"$PWCLI" snapshot
"$PWCLI" click e15
"$PWCLI" type "Playwright"
"$PWCLI" press Enter
"$PWCLI" screenshot
```

If the user prefers a global install, this is also valid:

```bash
npm install -g @playwright/cli@latest
playwright-cli --help
```

## Core workflow

1. Open the page.
2. Snapshot to get stable element refs.
3. Interact using refs from the latest snapshot.
4. Re-snapshot after navigation or significant DOM changes.
5. Capture artifacts (screenshot, pdf, traces) when useful.

Minimal loop:

```bash
"$PWCLI" open https://example.com
"$PWCLI" snapshot
"$PWCLI" click e3
"$PWCLI" snapshot
```

## When to snapshot again

Snapshot again after:

- navigation
- clicking elements that change the UI substantially
- opening/closing modals or menus
- tab switches

Refs can go stale. When a command fails due to a missing ref, snapshot again.

## Recommended patterns

### Form fill and submit

```bash
"$PWCLI" open https://example.com/form
"$PWCLI" snapshot
"$PWCLI" fill e1 "user@example.com"
"$PWCLI" fill e2 "password123"
"$PWCLI" click e3
"$PWCLI" snapshot
```

### Debug a UI flow with traces

```bash
"$PWCLI" open https://example.com --headed
"$PWCLI" tracing-start
# ...interactions...
"$PWCLI" tracing-stop
```

### Multi-tab work

```bash
"$PWCLI" tab-new https://example.com
"$PWCLI" tab-list
"$PWCLI" tab-select 0
"$PWCLI" snapshot
```

## Wrapper script

The wrapper script uses `npx --package @playwright/cli playwright-cli` so the CLI can run without a global install:

```bash
"$PWCLI" --help
```

Prefer the wrapper unless the repository already standardizes on a global install.

Open only what you need:

- CLI command reference: `references/cli.md`
- Practical workflows and troubleshooting: `references/workflows.md`

## Guardrails

- Always snapshot before referencing element ids like `e12`.
- Re-snapshot when refs seem stale.
- Prefer explicit commands over `eval` and `run-code` unless needed.
- When you do not have a fresh snapshot, use placeholder refs like `eX` and say why; do not bypass refs with `run-code`.
- Use `--headed` when a visual check will help.
- When capturing artifacts in this repo, use `output/playwright/` and avoid introducing new top-level artifact folders.
- Default to CLI commands and workflows, not Playwright test specs.

## Browser-friendly multistage search

Running the fine sample bank against every candidate is unnecessary.

### Coarse pass

```text
4,096 samples
128–256 candidates
```

Keep:

* top 16 candidates by new coverage,
* top 8 candidates by quality improvement,
* any candidates within 1 percentage point of the best union.

### Fine pass

Evaluate the survivors using 24,576 samples.

### Local refinement

Around the top four candidates, generate nearby positions at:

```text
±½ candidate spacing
±¼ candidate spacing
±⅛ candidate spacing
```

Test cardinal and diagonal offsets:

```text
+x, -x, +z, -z
+x+z, +x-z, -x+z, -x-z
```

Include vertical offsets only when the allowed origin volume permits them.

This gives a result that is not constrained to the initial grid.

# Algorithm 2: Jointly optimize both origins

This is a discrete **maximum union coverage** problem.

## Objective

For every pair of candidates `a` and `b`:

```text
PairCoverage(a,b) = coverage(a ∪ b)
```

For quality:

```text
PairQuality(a,b) =
    average over samples of max(Q(a,s), Q(b,s))
```

The important difference from sequential selection is that you do **not** first pick the strongest individual origin.

Two individually second-tier origins can jointly outperform the individually best origin plus any companion.

## Fast all-pairs search

With bitsets:

```ts
function pairCoverage(
  a: Uint32Array,
  b: Uint32Array,
  sampleCount: number,
): number {
  let covered = 0;

  for (let word = 0; word < a.length; word++) {
    covered += popcount32(a[word] | b[word]);
  }

  return covered / sampleCount;
}
```

For 256 candidates there are:

```text
256 × 255 ÷ 2 = 32,640 pairs
```

With 4,096 samples, each visibility bitset contains only 128 32-bit words. That makes the coarse all-pairs search very cheap once candidate visibility has been computed.

## Hard pair constraints

Reject pairs when:

```text
distance(a,b) < minimum separation
```

A useful default is:

```text
max(
  2 × candidate spacing,
  5–8% of scene diagonal
)
```

Do not make separation too large. In compact or highly occluded scenes, two relatively nearby origins on opposite sides of an occluding prop may genuinely be optimal.

There is normally no need for an explicit overlap penalty. Maximizing the union already rewards complementary coverage. Use overlap only as a tie-breaker.

## Coarse joint search

```ts
function rankAllPairs(
  evaluations: OriginEvaluation[],
  sampleCount: number,
): PairCandidate[] {
  const pairs: PairCandidate[] = [];

  for (let a = 0; a < evaluations.length; a++) {
    for (let b = a + 1; b < evaluations.length; b++) {
      const originA = evaluations[a];
      const originB = evaluations[b];

      if (!pairSeparationIsValid(originA, originB)) continue;

      const coverage = pairCoverage(
        originA.coverageBits,
        originB.coverageBits,
        sampleCount,
      );

      pairs.push({
        a,
        b,
        coverage,
      });
    }
  }

  pairs.sort((x, y) => y.coverage - x.coverage);
  return pairs;
}
```

Keep the top 12–20 pair seeds.

Do not shortlist candidates by individual coverage before testing pairs. That can remove a candidate with mediocre individual coverage but excellent complementarity.

## Fine pair search

Collect every unique origin appearing in the top coarse pairs, plus nearby candidate positions.

Re-evaluate these using the fine surface bank.

Then calculate:

```ts
function finePairMetrics(
  a: OriginEvaluation,
  b: OriginEvaluation,
): PairMetrics {
  let usableCount = 0;
  let totalQuality = 0;
  let overlapCount = 0;
  let aOnly = 0;
  let bOnly = 0;

  for (let i = 0; i < a.quality.length; i++) {
    const qa = a.quality[i];
    const qb = b.quality[i];

    const coveredA = qa >= USABLE_QUALITY_BYTE;
    const coveredB = qb >= USABLE_QUALITY_BYTE;

    if (coveredA || coveredB) usableCount++;
    if (coveredA && coveredB) overlapCount++;
    if (coveredA && !coveredB) aOnly++;
    if (!coveredA && coveredB) bOnly++;

    totalQuality += Math.max(qa, qb);
  }

  return {
    unionCoverage: usableCount / a.quality.length,
    overlapCoverage: overlapCount / a.quality.length,
    aOnlyCoverage: aOnly / a.quality.length,
    bOnlyCoverage: bOnly / a.quality.length,
    averageQuality:
      totalQuality / (255 * a.quality.length),
  };
}
```

Rank the fine pairs:

1. Maximum union coverage.
2. Within 0.25 percentage points, maximum average quality.
3. Then maximum minimum contribution:

```text
maximize min(A-only coverage, B-only coverage)
```

That last tie-break discourages one origin from doing almost everything while the other contributes a trivial amount.

## Continuous local refinement

For each of the top four fine pairs:

1. Hold origin B fixed.
2. Search small offsets around A.
3. Accept the best A.
4. Hold the new A fixed.
5. Search small offsets around B.
6. Accept the best B.
7. Halve the search radius.
8. Repeat three or four times.

```ts
for (const initialPair of topPairs) {
  let a = initialPair.positionA;
  let b = initialPair.positionB;
  let step = initialCandidateSpacing / 2;

  for (let level = 0; level < 4; level++) {
    a = optimizeLocalPosition(a, b, step);
    b = optimizeLocalPosition(b, a, step);
    step *= 0.5;
  }

  saveRefinedPair(a, b);
}
```

Use pattern search rather than gradient descent. Visibility changes discontinuously when a ray clears an edge, so the objective does not have a useful smooth gradient.

# Optional but strongly recommended: shot-weighted optimization

Total mesh area can reward surfaces that will never appear on camera.

Use two independent sample banks:

### Area bank

Uniform samples across the mesh.

```text
Measures literal geometric surface coverage.
```

### Shot bank

Generate samples by casting pixels from planned cameras into the set:

1. Sample each landed shot at low resolution.
2. For camera moves, sample several times along the path.
3. Raycast each selected pixel.
4. Save the first-hit world point and surface normal.
5. Repeat samples according to shot duration or importance.

Uniform image-pixel sampling naturally prioritizes surfaces occupying more screen space.

Then calculate:

```text
AreaCoverage(a,b)
ShotCoverage(a,b)
```

Suggested modes:

| Mode          | Area importance | Shot importance |
| ------------- | --------------: | --------------: |
| Total surface |            100% |              0% |
| Balanced      |             40% |             60% |
| Production    |             20% |             80% |

For the balanced mode:

```text
PrimaryScore =
    0.40 × AreaCoverage
  + 0.60 × ShotCoverage
```

Use projection quality as the secondary tie-breaker.

For PanoRef, I would make **Balanced** the default and let the user select **Maximize total surface area** explicitly.

---

# Calculate the reachable upper bound

Before judging whether the result is good, combine coverage from every valid candidate:

```ts
reachableBits = OR(allCandidateCoverageBits);
```

This estimates the maximum surface area reachable from the permitted origin region.

Report:

```text
Pair coverage:               81%
Reachable from allowed area: 88%
Pair captures:               92% of reachable surface
Unreachable surface:         12%
```

This distinction is extremely useful. It tells you whether:

* the pair selection is weak, or
* the remaining geometry simply cannot be seen from any legal panorama origin.

The optimizer should not spend effort pursuing cabinet undersides, sealed backs, internal geometry, or surfaces outside the allowed capture volume.

---

# Coverage visualization

After optimization, assign each fine sample one of five states:

| State        | Meaning                               |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| A only       | Covered only by origin A              |
| B only       | Covered only by origin B              |
| Both         | Covered by either origin              |
| Poor quality | Visible but grazing or under-resolved |
| Uncovered    | Occluded from both                    |

Render these as a temporary vertex/triangle heatmap. That gives immediate visual feedback about whether the mathematical optimum is sensible.

The results panel should display:

```text
Origin A usable coverage
Origin B usable coverage

B-only coverage
Overlap
```

{"content": [{"text": "Yes—this is now a real implementation of the algorithm, not merely the occlusion foundation. The latest head adds 17 coverage-engine files, a worker, UI, and tests. Joint mode genuinely evaluates candidate pairs rather than greedily selecting the best first origin.

Revised verdict

Algorithm architecture for normal graybox sets: 8/10

Correctness of the two search modes: 7.5/10

Readiness for complex imported sets: 4/10

Overall: promising, but I would not merge it as production-ready yet.


The math/search design is mostly right. The blockers are implementation scale and one dangerous workflow decision.

What it got right

The surface sampler is deterministic and correctly samples triangles in proportion to world-space area using barycentric coordinates.

Origin evaluation includes:

actual segment occlusion,

geometric face normals,

viewing angle,

approximate projected texel density,

separate visibility and usable-coverage bitsets,

continuous quality values.


That closely follows the algorithm we designed.

The joint-pair mode is genuinely joint. It checks every legal coarse pair, ranks them by bitset union, and only then applies quality and contribution tie-breakers. It does not discard individually mediocre but complementary origins prematurely.

The shared coarse-to-fine engine is also sensibly organized:

4,096 coarse samples,

256 candidates,

retained pair seeds,

24,576 fine samples,

local offsets,

separate fixed-first and joint branches.


The tests cover deterministic sampling, double-sided occlusion, marginal second-origin ranking, non-greedy pair ranking, candidate generation, and both search modes.

Blockers

1. Imported sets can produce zero legal candidates

This is the biggest correctness issue.

For every non-floor scene object, the extractor stores the entire object’s axis-aligned bounding box as an obstacle.

Candidate clearance is then the distance from the origin point to those bounding boxes, and candidates within 0.3 meters are rejected. A point anywhere inside an AABB has a distance of zero.

Consider a typical imported model:

Imported Set
├── floor
├── walls
├── furniture
└── props

PanoRef represents that as one imported SceneObject. Its AABB may enclose the entire room. Every sensible camera origin inside the room is therefore “inside the obstacle bounds,” gets zero clearance, and is rejected.

This can affect:

a complete Maya set imported as one GLB,

a room shell and furniture combined into one mesh,

concave geometry,

L-shaped walls,

any large model whose AABB contains empty navigable space.


Fix

Use actual geometry clearance, not object AABBs:

candidate valid =
    camera sphere/capsule does not intersect nearby triangles

The coverage BVH can support this through point-to-triangle distance, sphere intersection, or a shapecast. At minimum, obstacle bounds should be per connected mesh or spatial cluster—not per imported set object.

Add a regression test with one imported object containing a room floor, walls, and empty interior.

2. The geometry representation will not scale to heavy imports

Every triangle is expanded into a JavaScript object containing:

three independent Vec3 arrays,

a normal array,

IDs,

area.


For 3 million triangles, even an ideal packed representation would require approximately:

Positions: 3,000,000 × 9 × 4 bytes = 108 MB
Normals:   3,000,000 × 3 × 4 bytes =  36 MB
                                           ──────
Minimum packed geometry data:              144 MB

The actual representation uses JavaScript objects, arrays, and 64-bit numbers, so it will be several times larger. It is then structured-cloned into the worker with postMessage, temporarily creating another enormous representation.

The BVH also recursively sorts and slices JavaScript index arrays.

Worse, every triangle intersection allocates several temporary three-element arrays. Millions of candidate/sample raycasts will create extreme garbage-collection pressure.

This will probably work on the default graybox. I would expect serious freezing, memory spikes, or crashes on the heavy imported projects that previously hit PanoRef’s multi-million-triangle limits.

Fix

Use compact typed arrays:

interface PackedCoverageGeometry {
  positions: Float32Array;
  indices: Uint32Array;
  normals?: Float32Array;
  meshRanges: Uint32Array;
  transforms: Float32Array;
}

Transfer ArrayBuffers into the worker rather than cloning nested objects.

For the BVH, either:

use three-mesh-bvh,

implement a flat typed-array BVH with in-place partitioning,

or build per-mesh BVHs from the existing indexed geometries.


Also avoid expanding indexed vertices into three world-space vertex arrays per triangle.

3. Geometry extraction still blocks the main thread

The panel synchronously calls extractCoverageScene(project) before creating/posting to the worker.

So the worker keeps the expensive optimizer off the UI thread, but not:

scene recreation,

triangle flattening,

world-transform application,

geometry disposal,

structured cloning.


On a complex model, the app may freeze before the worker even reports its first progress event.

The extraction itself needs to move into the worker, or at least become chunked and yield between meshes.

4. “Apply to selected panorama pair” is conceptually wrong

The UI allows the optimized origins to be written directly into the two existing panorama references.

The workspace handler literally changes their stored origins:

updatePanoReference(primaryPanoId, { origin: originA });
updatePanoReference(secondaryPanoId, { origin: originB });

But an existing panorama was rendered or generated from its original origin. Changing its metadata does not transform the image into a panorama captured from the new position. It merely projects the old pixels from the wrong point, ruining alignment.

Correct workflow

For fixed-first:

1. Preserve the existing panorama and its origin.


2. Move the next capture origin to B.


3. Render a new graybox panorama.


4. Inpaint/generate the new styled panorama.


5. Import it as the secondary panorama.



For joint mode:

1. Create a two-origin capture plan.


2. Move capture origin to A.


3. Capture/render A.


4. Move to B.


5. Capture/render B.


6. Associate each imported result with its actual origin.



Do not rewrite the origins of already captured panoramas.

5. The reachable upper bound is mathematically inconsistent

reachableCoverage is calculated using the coarse sample bank and all coarse candidates.

The final combined coverage is calculated using a different fine sample bank generated with seed + 1.

Those two percentages are then placed together in the same result and used to calculate reachable efficiency.

Therefore, the UI can theoretically show:

Combined coverage:        83%
Reachable upper bound:    80%
Reachable captured:      100%

The clamp hides the impossible ratio but does not repair the incompatible estimates.

There is another fixed-first issue: the reachable set is calculated before the arbitrary first origin is evaluated, so the fixed first origin is not included in the reachable upper bound at all.

Fix

Use a common validation sample bank for both:

final pair coverage,

reachable candidate union,

efficiency.


For fixed-first, include the fixed origin in the reachable union.

You can still use separate coarse and fine search banks internally, but reported metrics must be evaluated on one shared final bank.

# Bug Fix Verification

Fix the reported defect through a disciplined reproduce-isolate-repair-verify workflow. Optimize for a minimal root-cause fix and a durable regression test.

## 1. Define the failure

Extract or establish:

- expected behavior,
- actual behavior,
- reproduction steps,
- affected environment or configuration,
- frequency and scope,
- relevant logs, errors, screenshots, inputs, or data.

Use existing evidence first. Ask a question only when missing information materially prevents a safe reproduction; otherwise proceed with a clearly stated assumption.

## 2. Reproduce before editing

When feasible:

- run the smallest command, test, request, or user flow that demonstrates the bug,
- capture the exact failure evidence,
- distinguish the reported symptom from the underlying cause,
- note when reproduction is impossible because of missing services, credentials, hardware, data, or environment constraints.

Do not spend excessive effort recreating an unavailable production environment when a focused local test can represent the failure.

## 3. Isolate the root cause

- Trace only the relevant execution path first.
- Inspect recent or related changes when useful.
- Compare working and failing inputs or states.
- Form a falsifiable hypothesis before modifying code.
- Use targeted instrumentation or temporary diagnostics when needed, then remove them unless they provide lasting value.
- Avoid broad refactors until the root cause is understood.

## 4. Add a regression test

When feasible, create the narrowest meaningful test that:

- fails for the reproduced bug before the fix,
- passes after the fix,
- asserts externally meaningful behavior rather than implementation trivia,
- covers the relevant edge or failure condition,
- follows existing test conventions.

If an automated regression test is not feasible, state why and define a repeatable manual verification procedure.

## 5. Implement the minimal root-cause fix

- Correct the cause, not merely the visible symptom.
- Preserve unrelated behavior and public contracts.
- Avoid unrelated cleanup and speculative redesign.
- Update docs only when the fix changes documented behavior, limitations, setup, configuration, or user guidance.
- Add defensive handling only when it reflects a real supported case rather than hiding invalid state.

## 6. Verify and repair

Run in this order:

1. the regression test or focused reproduction,
2. directly related tests,
3. relevant lint/type/build checks,
4. the original runtime reproduction when practical,
5. broader validation only when the fix affects shared or cross-cutting code.

If validation fails:

- inspect the exact output,
- determine whether the failure is caused by the fix,
- revise the hypothesis or implementation,
- rerun the smallest relevant check,
- avoid repeating an expensive command without a new change or hypothesis.

Do not weaken tests or swallow errors to obtain a passing result.

## 7. Confirm non-regression

Verify that:

- the original failure no longer occurs,
- the intended path still works,
- the regression test would have caught the old behavior,
- directly adjacent behavior remains intact,
- no temporary diagnostics or accidental changes remain.

## 8. Final response format

### Root cause
Explain the specific cause and why it produced the symptom.

### Fix
State what changed and why it is the smallest appropriate correction.

### Regression coverage
Describe the test added or updated and what it proves.

### Verification
List commands and runtime reproduction results, including failures encountered and repaired.

### Documentation
State what changed, or why no update was needed.

### Remaining limitations
Include only genuine blockers or unverified conditions.

The Projected Style panel now feeds both dual-origin search modes from one coverage-analysis engine under `src/engine/projectionCoverage/`. The engine flattens the rendered solid meshes into world-space triangles, samples them deterministically by surface area, and uses a double-sided BVH segment query to reject occluded samples. Geometric face angle and approximate equirectangular texel density distinguish usable coverage from merely visible grazing surfaces.

- **Fixed-first:** evaluates the selected primary panorama origin and ranks second origins by combined usable coverage, then quality gain, overlap, and clearance.
- **Joint-pair:** ranks all coarse origin pairs by their coverage bitset union before fine evaluation, preserving candidates that are weak alone but complementary together.
- **Search:** automatically derives candidates from upward-facing floors, rejects them with triangle-accurate camera clearance, evaluates 4,096 coarse samples, iteratively recenters four local refinement levels, and reports final pair plus reachable union on one shared 24,576-sample bank. Fixed-first applies the same minimum-separation rule as joint mode.
- **Runtime isolation:** indexed positions, indices, mesh transforms, and floor ranges are stored in typed arrays. Main-thread extraction yields between objects and large buffer chunks, then transfers the ArrayBuffers to a module worker. The worker builds a flat typed-array BVH with in-place partitioning and allocation-free ray/clearance queries.
- **Application:** results are capture-plan positions only. They can move the graybox capture origin to A or B so a new panorama can be rendered, styled, and imported. Existing panorama references remain immutable because changing their stored origin would misproject the already-captured pixels.
- **Rendering parity:** dual-projector blending uses the same face-angle and approximate texel-density quality model as optimization, with winner-takes-most weighting; the coverage preview adds orange for visible but under-resolved/grazing surfaces.

UI fidelity and browser tests assert that optimization never rewrites existing panorama origins. `docs/coverage-optimizer-benchmark.md` records the repeatable real imported production-set benchmark.
